title: Where does Back take you?
hook: Back, back, then a new page. Then Back again. You might not land where you expect.

knows: visiting web pages and pressing Back
putting things on a pile and taking the top one off
doesNotKnow: that visiting a page after going back discards the forward pages

misconception: Back always returns to the page you looked at just before, retracing the order you visited them.
objective: The learner can explain that browser history behaves like a stack: Back steps down the pile, and visiting a new page after going back throws away the pages above, so after A, B, C, D, Back twice and E, Back lands on B.

claims.text: After visiting A, B, C, D, pressing Back twice, visiting E and pressing Back once, you are on B.
claims.source: Pile A, B, C, D (on D) -> Back -> C -> Back -> B -> visit E discards C and D, pile A, B, E -> Back -> B. Builder ran the stack trace in Node.

claims.text: After going back, the later pages are kept for Forward until you visit a new page, which throws them away.
claims.source: WHATWG HTML Living Standard, 'Session history' / 'navigables': navigating a traversable removes the session history entries after the current one ('forward' entries) before appending the new entry.

claims.text: A stack gives back the last thing added first (last in, first out); a queue gives back the first thing added first (first in, first out), like a line at a till.
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed., 10.1 'Stacks and queues': a stack implements a last-in, first-out policy; a queue implements first-in, first-out.

claims.text: The stage models history as one pile and has no Forward button; it shows forward pages as dashed entries above the current page.
claims.source: Demo.tsx: pages array plus a current index; visit() truncates above the index before pushing. A simplification of browser session history (claim c2).

recall.question: You read pages P, Q, R. You press Back once (to Q) and open a new page S. Which pages can Back and Forward now reach?
options: Back to Q and P; R is gone
Back to R, Q and P
Forward to R, back to Q and P
recall.why: History is a stack. Opening S from Q throws away R, which was above Q, and puts S on top: the pile is P, Q, S.
